My conception of the house at the present time is that there is taking place a realignment of forces. I am not surprised at the stand taken by the members of the group to my right on the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment, because the forces of reaction in this country are being lined up; the issues are becoming clearer; the lines are becoming more sharply drawn. There is no third course in my opinion as far as Canada and its future is concerned. Either you stand for the necessary social changes to guarantee the full implementation of the objectives for which we are fighting this war. or you believe in a continuance of the conditions that brought about the war. My conception of the stand taken by the party to my right is they are quite prepared to hang on to the old machine. They are not prepared to make any basic changes which would eliminate in the future the conditions we are experiencing at the present time. I think the alignment is a logical one and that the party to my right are taking the course which they would be expected to take.
They are not proposing in their amendment anything that is not being done already by the government. If all they want, is compulsion to use the full man-power and woman-power of this country, that is already being done in every field in which it can be done. There is ample evidence of that in the numerous orders in council which have been passed and in press statements which have been issued. Anyone in this house could prove within fifteen minutes that that is now being done by the government in every field in which it is possible to do it. The only thing the government is not doing is the things that were advocated in the amendment to the amendment proposed by this group, and our friends to my right are not prepared to make any changes in that direction or in any direction. I shall say no more on that.
My main reason for rising this afternoon is to defend the people whom I think I represent directly in the house, and that is the members of the unions, and particularly the Canadian Congress of Labour and its affiliates in the United States. The member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) in addressing the house on February 16, as reported at page 486 of Hansard, interpreted the labour policy of the Winnipeg convention,
and evidently he did it writh the full approval of every member of the group with which he sits.
He attacks the Congress for Industrial Organization in Canada. I said a moment ago that it was an uninformed attack. I said it for this reason-and I think it is something that should be clearly understood. The C.I.O., for the information of my friends to the right, is not a union. It has no union functions. It does not make nor does it negotiate contracts. The C.I.O. is the legislative centre in the United States to which the unions in that field are affiliated, and the C.I.O. in the United States carries on the legislative activities necessary to the movement in that country. It has no function whatever in Canada. The Canadian Congress of Labour in this country is the parallel organization to the C.I.O. in the United States, and all this drivel which the member for Parkdale talks, taking his cue from advertisements that are circulated throughout the country at this time with reference to the C.I.O., is irrevelant, inasmuch as that organization does not exist in Canada.
A few years ago the cry was communism. Any time you tried to exercise your rights as a citizen in the field of collective bargaining, you were considered a communist. Well, Russia has become respectable and it is not popular now to attack her, so that the slogan, particularly in the province of Ontario, is the C.I.O. Evidently the hon. member had the endorsation of the rest of his party in that regard because no exception was taken to his statement. The Canadian Congress of Labour to-day have 150,000 members in Canada. They have an affiliation with the other legislative body in the United States, and when that organization was attacked, the hon. membfer for Parkdale attacked the organized steel workers of Canada from coast to coast, the organized mine workers from coast to coast, the organized packing house workers, the textile workers, the united electrical workers. Every one of these organizations which he condemns so roundly as agitators and disrupters of industrial peace in Canada is thoroughly organized and is doing a good job in this country, and if there were more of them and they had more cooperation in that field from the powers that be there would be less strife. It is the fight put up by those who will not grant the workers of the country their day in court, which every other section of society enjoys, that is responsible for most of the turmoil that exists to-day.
I am glad that the member for Parkdale has put this on the record, because at the
The Address-Mr. Gillis

Winnipeg convention, while there was much talk about the right of the workers to organize, and all that kind of stuff, and how their heart bled and what they were prepared to do for the working people of their country, their official pronouncements in this house should be a clear indication to everyone in Canada that while they are still in opposition they are not ready, even for the sake of fooling the people, to make gestures in the direction of the right of the workers to bargain. What would be the situation if they were on the other -side of the house and had the right to make laws? Evidently their programme at Winnipeg, as far as its practical application is concerned, is company unionism, because the hon. member paid tribute in that speech to company unionism in this country.
The other evening I called the attention of the Prime Minister to this advertisement that has been circulated in every newspaper in Canada. It was put out by the Steel Company of Canada, with a personal letter from R. H. McMaster, president. I took exception to that for this reason. The responsible people connected with the trade union movement in this country are desirous of seeing our war effort promoted; they are not desirous of seeing strikes, confusion and everything else that goes with it; and when the Prime Minister made the statement that a new board was being set up, a new jurisprudence for labour in Canada was being established, and that the new board would function as an industrial court, I thought it was bad taste for the Steel Company of Canada to take the attitude it did. I thought so in view of the fact that newsprint is rationed in Canada. Moreover, my suspicion is that the taxpayers of Canada are paying for this advertising, because advertising is a part of operating cost, and is deducted from the corporation tax. Just before that court even got started, a tense labour dispute was going on in Canada, an ultimation having been given that if, within a reasonable time, a peaceful solution was not arrived at we were likely to have a repetition of what was gone through in the steel workers' strike. I thought it was ill advised on the part of the government not to take note of the fact that the steel company was circulating that advertisement throughout the length and breadth of Canada, provoking the steel workers, provoking the organized labour movement, and at the same time making the taxpayers pay for it. The member for Parkdale complimented the steel company upon its action. He thinks it was a wonderful thing. If that is part of the Winnipeg convention's attitude
[Mr. Gillis.)
towards the working people of the country, then I think it is time we found it out and governed ourselves accordingly.
In the field of compulsion, here is a newspaper dispatch from the Sudbury Star of Saturday, February 13. This horrible C.I.O. in the mines and steel plants and in the essential industries that are working, some of them, sixteen hours a day, are frozen to their jobs. They stay on the job. They are not permitted to change their job. In this order which I have here they are placed in this position-and I think it is something of which the government should take cognizance. The order of October 24, 1942, which brought about the means of holding labour to the production of important commodities in these essential industries, has been extended, and these people, whom the member for Parkdale classifies as agitators and disturbers of the peace, are placed in this position now. Those employed in essential industries are given deferment for military call, but that deferment is in the hands of the employer. The employer says^ whether you are to be called for military service or not, and evidently that power is being used, particularly in Sudbury in the nickel industry. It puts a weapon in the hands of the employer. If you happen to join an organization which he does not like, he can immediately notify the selective service board that your deferment should be discontinued and that you should be called for military service. If you are not exactly the kind of employee he thinks you should be, he has the right to see that you are called for military service. If that is not sufficient compulsion in the field of man-power, you have conscription in Canada not only for military service but for all essential industries.
On this question of national selective service may I make this statement, seeing that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is in the house. I followed closely the controversy between the Department of Labour and Elliott Little. I think there is room in Canada for a thorough overhauling of our national selective service regulations. Many things are happening that should not happen. For example, the wartime prices and trade board has been given authority to close out some
20,000	small industries in Canada-non-essential industries, they are declared to be-and you will find that many of these non-essential industries are highly unionized. For a period of years they built up certain wage schedules for themselves. When that industry is closed out under the present selective service regulations, these men will be relegated to the ranks of the unemployed.

The Address-Mr. Gilhs
They must go then to the national selective service offices and make application for employment in an essential industry. They carry with them none of the wage rates they have been able to build up over a period of years. While they may have been receiving 85 cents or a dollar an hour at some skilled occupation that is not to-day essential, they are obliged at times to go into a war plant and start as apprentices at 42 cents an hour; they lose the standard of living that they have built up through their own struggles over a long time, and nothing is done to protect them. To boil the thing down to plain and simple terms, I cannot see how the Minister of Labour could for a moment imagine that Mr. Little's proposals and the powers he asked for in connection with national selective service were in any sense dictatorial. I think the reverse is true; that the dictatorial powers that Mr. Little was accused of asking for are operating to-day in the selective service as administered by the Department of Labour.
My conception of Mr. Little's proposals is that he was prepared to accept full responsibility in that field, and he wanted the authority to do so. If an industry was closed out he wanted to make sure, before four or five hundred men were thrown into unemployment, that there was employment for these men. and that in the turnover they went from one industry to the other en bloc. In addition he wanted to protect the wage rates built up over a period of years in industries considered to-day non-essential. He did not want to reduce the standard of living of men or women who were obliged to change their employment because of the exigencies of war. That is my plain and simple conception of Mr. Little's proposals in the field of selective service.
I am not blaming the Minister of Labour; he is only one man and the problem is a big one. It is one with which someone who has technical and practical experience, which I think Mr. Little had, should be given full power to deal.
When Mr. Little first came to Ottawa we advocated in the house that he should be freed from war service regulations under that department. In addition we said he should be freed from any supervision or influence by the Department of Labour in connection with the mobilization of man-power for war service; that the transfer of man-power from coast to coast was a job that required a fulltime administrator, and that he should have some latitude with respect to the administration of these regulations. The whole thing to-day is in a knot; from coast to coast there is chaos. I do not say that to be critical. I moved about the country considerably last summer, and I ran into it. If anyone here has any doubt about how it is working I would advise him to call at the Spadina avenue office of the selective service in Toronto and have a look. I do not say that the Minister of Labour can go there and kick that loose, but I do say that someone down there should have some authority to do something. Before there can be any success in the field of selective service someone will have to be appointed full time and be given full authority to make the necessary changes in the way I think Mr. Little proposed making them. When 20.000 non-essential industries are being closed out it is a big job, affecting the livelihood of a great many people. It is throwing out of the field completely a large number of men who have quite an investment in their businesses, and that is something which requires careful consideration.
I do not think anyone should take the stand in this house that you or I should be asked to reduce our standard of living fifty per cent in any transfer from non-essential to essential employment. If that were done with contractors who are building airports and ships and all that kind of thing, I would say yes; we would be quite prepared to make the same sacrifice that the other man is making. But when a man is working for a wage which just enables him to live from day to day, and he is told that he must leave that employment, discontinue all his associations, and be transferred to another section of the country and another line of work, and at the same time reduce his standard of living at least fifty per cent-I can name industries where that has actually taken place-the Department of Labour would be well advised to do something along the lines suggested by Mr. Little.
There are many more things I should like to say but I shall not detain the house any longer. I rose this afternoon simply to say something for the people whom I think I directly represent here. I belong to that outlaw organization of which the hon. member for Parkdale speaks-those troublemakers. I have belonged to the mine workers' organization for the past twenty-five years. Unfortunately the working people of this country have not many agencies that will take up their cause. The press of this country belongs to the people represented here by the hon. member for Parkdale; the radio is largely in their hands; the House of Commons is largely in their hands. They have many spokesmen here, while unfortunately the people I attempt to speak for have very few agencies through which they can defend themselves.
The Address-Mr. Blackmore

I hear someone mention this committee of two hundred in Toronto. That committee does not consist entirely of Conservatives; there are as many reactionary so-called Liberals in it as there are Tories. My friends on this side and my friends over there who really believe that we are fighting a war to do away with wars in the future will have to begin to understand that the machine at the top, the small invisible government of this country, has no politics. They are not Liberals; they are not tories; their aim is power and direction from behind the scenes. Let everyone in this house understand that, and make this House of Commons supreme in legislating for the people. If while we are fighting the war it is necessary to have controls-and it is- let the members of the house use their voices in this house and out of it, to see to it that the people they directly represent here are given some share in the controls behind the scenes, in order that we may come out of this war with a free and democratic parliament. I am doubtful about it now, judging from the trend of events.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before dealing with the amendment to the amendment I wish to refer briefly to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Since I came to parliament I have never heard the Prime Minister in such fine form as he displayed this afternoon. It really deserves note, I believe, that a man who is advancing in years is so full of fire and energy and able to give a good rousing talk on such short notice.
The Prime Minister said one or two things of which I believe every hon. member should take special note. He had a good deal to say about the formation of new parties, and seemed to be disposed to lay the blame for the formation of new parties on the people who form them. May I point out, however, that the Prime Minister completely missed the boat. He placed the blame just where it should not be. He referred to Prance; what caused the fall of France? Was it the new parties that arose, or was it the dead old-line parties that stood stolid and utterly refused to change, no matter what happened? Their leaders were dead; the majority of the people behind them were dead, and when the impact of war came upon them it became clear that they were dead. Let me point out that it is generally accepted and is coming to be more generally accepted in this country that the two old-line parties in this country are dead, root and branch; that the leaders and the prominent men in both of them, as well as the powers behind the scenes to which the hon. member for (Mr. Gillis.]
Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has just referred, are dead. This means only that though they are not dead to their own interests they are utterly dead to the interests of the people of the country which they have undertaken to rule.
Now I ask the Prime Minister to take a few minutes' even in his busy life to tell me what possible recourse the Canadian people have if they find that whichever old-line party is in power betrays their interests and fails to keep its promises. What other recourse have the people but to organize new parties? The organization of new parties stands as a condemnation of the policies or administration of the old-line parties, in whatever countries the new parties are organized.
I think it would be a good thing to refer just for a moment to the Prime Minister's appeal to the members of his party to support him. I am unable to tell whether he was trying to intimidate the members of the house by holding forth the threat of an election, or some such thing. If he was; if he thought that by going to the country he would remove from his side several thorns which are now beginning to hurt considerably, I believe he is very much mistaken. Anyone who would imagine that a new election would remove from this parliament gentlemen like the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) and others, had better do a little more studying. The Prime Minister may have been indicating that he was weary of it all and would probably resign. I would sympathize more with him if I had not heard his speech this afternoon, but considering the energy and power he then manifested I believe he is quite capable of carrying on even through another plebiscite, should that become necessary. The Prime Minister asked for the responsibility that he now has. He organized for it; he and his party henchmen did everything in their power at the last election to get it. I think the Canadian people are thoroughly justified in expecting him to stand right up to the task and carry through the responsibility which he very willingly assumed.
This house must make two very important decisions with respect to the subamendment. The first is, what are we going to do with the subamendment itself? That is a relatively easy question to deal with, but the second one is not so simple. What are members of this house to do about the causes that produced the subamendment? That is a matter not to be

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
disposed of so easily. I should like to give some attention to the answers to these questions. First, I should like to turn to the question of the subamendment. As I see it, the plebiscite on which we spent so much time last year was designed to answer the question raised by the amendment to the amendment. A "yes" vote was generally understood to mean the willingness of the voter to give the government freedom to introduce conscription for overseas service. Canadians as a whole definitely voted "yes". A majority in Quebec voted "no", which was theif absolute privilege and one which they should be free to exercise without any abuse from any organ or any person in the country. In accordance with the expressed will of the majority of the voters the .government introduced Bill No. 80, which modified the National Resources Mobilization Act in order to give the government freedom to introduce conscription for overseas service. This house voted on Bill No. 80 as follows. After having told the people, through their leader, to vote "yes" on the plebiscite; after having helped the Canadian people, therefore, to vote "yes", the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation came into this house and voted "no" on the bill based upon the plebiscite. Many of my fellow Canadians who speak French, among them being the mover of the amendment to the amendment, also voted against .Bill No. 80. The total vote against that bill was fifty-four, so that there was hardly any doubt as to how the house stood with respect to that measure. In view of the fact that the country voted "yes" and this house voted "yes", I fail to see how, in the short space of time that has intervened, this house could possibly reverse its position and support the amendment to the amendment.
Our group, the social crediters, are committed to vote against the amendment to the amendment because of several things in our history. There has been some sort of attempt on the part of this group to be consistent, and on at least certain matters I think we have been consistent ever since we went into Canadian public life. In 1937 I issued a statement to the press to the effect that I was going to support the government's proposal to increase the defence estimates. When those estimates came up I voted in favour of them, indicating quite clearly that I believed Canada should be prepared to offer effective cooperation in the defence of the British commonwealth and all that it holds dear. When the war broke out, this group took a stand in favour of unreserved cooperation with the British commonwealth of nations until victory should be won. Again, when the National Resources Mobilization Act was introduced in 1940 we supported
the principle of the mobilization of all the resources of this country, in order that we might build up a powerful force with which to fight to foe. When the plebiscite question was up for discussion I, representing this group, did not tell the Canadian people how to vote. We took the view that it was not the prerogative of any group or party in this house to tell the Canadian people how they ought to vote on a question so vitally important as the matter of conscription. We simply outlined certain problems involved and left the people to form their own decisions. When the Canadian people voted we held ourselves, as the democratic representatives of democratic people, bound to vote as the people required we should vote. Thus when Bill No. 80 came up this group voted for it, and therefore supported the change in the mobilization act which gave the government power to apply conscription.
My group will continue to vote "yes", in favour of the mobilization of the resources of this country. There is no change in the condition since last year which in any way could justify our reversing our decision. The national existence of the British commonwealth is at stake, a point which I am afraid some hon. members forget. The national existence of all the nations of North America is at stake, and that includes both English-! speaking and French-speaking people, both in Canada and in the United States.
The foe continues dreadfully powerful and, in the main, victorious still; and stern, with an almost fanatical determination to win, a sort of frenzy generated by despair. I think we can hardly expect a crack-up in our enemy such as favoured us during the last war. They are fighting with their backs to the wall. All these matters should, I believe, persuade anyone to vote for the greatest possible measure of strengthening of the government's hands in the conduct of the conflict.
The good which could be accomplished by the passage of the subamendment could not possibly compensate for the inestimable harm which would result. I think in his most thoughtful moments even the mover of the subamendment would agree that that is so. Social crediters therefore will vote against the amendment to the amendment.
May I turn now for a short time to the consideration of a problem which, in my opinion, should exercise the house deeply, namely, the discussion of the cause which resulted in one who was a trusted colleague of the Prime Minister, one who has been honoured and respected from coast to coast in Canada, moving an amendment to the
The Address-Mr. Blackmore

amendment amounting to a vote of want of confidence in this Liberal government. That cause cannot be brushed aside lightly, nor can it be scoffed away.
What caused the situation which faces us in Canada? I believe all Canadians, both English- and French-speaking, should bear in mind that fundamentally the thing which caused the feeling we have to-day was a thing over which none of us had any control whatsoever. It was the. fact that the British perhaps happened-I cannot say that is correct, at this distance-to be fortunate in winning the conflict of 1759. In the peace treaty they were given the responsibility of helping to govern the lives of a great many people extracted from a race which for centuries must have been the traditional enemy of the British people. Let us face that situation squarely, and without passion or prejudice. Let us make allowance for the feeling which must have passed on naturally from father to son, through the generations. That was the first cause of the present condition.
The second is one over which perhaps no one in this house could have exercised much control, but over which perhaps all can exercise some control in the future. I refer to the knavish tricks of politics. If I am correctly informed, there has been carried on among the French-Canadian people-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What kind of politics?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I shall enlarge upon that matter shortly. I refer to the intrigue, machinations and even downright treachery by ignorant and even knavish politicians, whose efforts did not add to the knowledge of French Canadians respecting the new situation in which they found themselves; did not add to the understanding of British institutions and the purpose of the British empire, including the whole set-up in which we must live our lives; did not add to the confidence those people could feel in their English-speaking compatriots in Canada. I believe that a large part of the blame for that unfortunate ill-feeling, which at least in some measure exists in Canada, must be laid at the door of those unscrupulous men whom, on the floor of the house, I have called shysters. And before leaving that point may I add that the shysters were not all Liberals or all Conservatives.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Many of them were.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They were both.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Social Credit party was not in existence at the time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I may add that the Social Credit party had nothing to do with it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not at that time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, nor now. If your people are carrying on down there under Social Credit, then they are basing everything they have to say on the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and are not engaging in any measures designed to arouse passion, prejudice or ill-feeling. There is plenty of evidence of that. I may say that the only group in the house which from the time of its entry up to the present has seen practically just what was going to happen, and which then stood for the very things for which it stands to-day, and consequently has a record for consistency not paralleled anywhere in the British empire, is the Social Credit group. You can be pretty certain they were not entirely blind when they first formed their party, some eight or nine years ago. They had some vision.
May I turn now to the third cause of the unhappy condition which exists in parts of Canada with respect to differences of race? For some reason after the last war there was sown in Canada from coast to coast one of the most pernicious forms of propaganda in favour of pacifism that one can conceive. I believe every hon. member should study seriously that propaganda with a view to finding out where it originated. It completely blinded the people of Canada and, as hon. members of the Liberal party know very well, the result of that blindness was that many men stood in the house and fought against armaments, against participation in any war to come, and all that sort of thing-only to find that they had been completely deceived. That pacifistic propaganda went throughout the length and breadth of French as well as English Canada. That malady of pacifism did not affect the French-Canadian people any more thoroughly than it did the Englishspeaking Canadian people. It had a part to play in the plebiscite for which the Prime Minister worked last year. It had a part to play in the delivery of his speech this afternoon. It had a great deal to do with the abuse which he has suffered.
The fourth cause of this unhappy condition I think must be called by just what it is, a lack of vision and understanding on the part of the Prime Minister. I am not suggesting that he was insincere, but I will say that if we may judge from his pronouncements, as referred to with such passion and justice by some hon. members to my left, he lacked vision and understanding of the things which might come to pass in this country. The

Precedence of Government Motions
result was that where he should have given strong, courageous and understanding leadership, he failed to do so and is now suffering the consequences.
The fifth cause is the Liberal stand from generation to generation, particularly during the last twenty-five years. I do not desire to say anything offensive, but I think they will have to grant, as hon. members to my left declared last night, that they deceived the people of French Canada into thinking for twenty-five years that if they just persisted in electing Liberals they never would have conscription. I suppose some of the most ardent devotees even told- the people that they would never have war, that we would never participate in a war, and all that sort of simple foolishness. There was no justification for any man over sixteen years of age with any degree of intelligence ever forming a conclusion that we in this country could be free from war. Yet the Liberal party deluded the people from end to end of this country for twenty-five years into thinking that by electing them they would be putting in power magicians who could keep us out of war. No wonder that they were believed, but no wonder that disappointment is so general, resulting even in the mild amendment to the amendment which we are now discussing! .
The sixth cause of our difficulty must be recognized as the suddenness, the strength and the fury of the attack by the foe. I had every confidence that we were going to be attacked, but I must say that I was never able to find evidence to show me how terrible the attack would be when it came. The fury of that attack placed the Canadian people as a whole, along with all other British peoples, in a most painful situation.
This brought about the seventh cause of our difficulty, which was the consequent need of Canada to leap as it were from a weak peacetime position into a great warlike exertion. Many soldiers had to be had. At the same time we were expanding our food production, our munitions production and every other activity in our industrial and economic life. What could the government in Canada do? I think hon. members will all recognize that I am in no way minimizing the blame attached to the Prime Minister, but neither am I going to exaggerate it. I want to give him the benefit of the doubt. I say, even although I am in the opposition, I do not feel that much of the abuse which has been hurled at that man's head is justifiable. He found himself in an exceedingly difficult position; I think far too little allowance has been made for that, perhaps from all sides of the house.
What could he do? What could the administration do? It had to have men, and a large part of the people of Canada had been deluded into thinking that conscription would never be used. It was almost sacrilege to mention it. His own party had committed themselves and they did so again in 1940. In many instances members occupying seats on the government side obtained those seats because of their pledge against conscription. The result was that the Prime Minister found himself in an almost impossible position. Men had to be had, but he was denied the privilege of using conscription even when the plebiscite had been voted upon. What could he do? The result was, as the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) pointed out last night, that there have been abuses in our efforts to raise man-power in this country, which I think probably five generations of Canadians will not live down.

Before I move the adjournment of the house I have a motion which I should like to place before the house. I move:
That the order passed on the twenty-eighth of January, 1943, giving precedence to the debate on the address be suspended until next Tuesday, the twenty-third of February instant.
The purpose of this motion is to enable us on Monday next to make headway with some of the motions on the order paper with respect to the appointment of select committees. If this motion carries, I shall indicate the order in which the various items on the agenda will be taken up.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER FEBRUARY 22
speechtext:
Hon. members will see in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday that I give notice:
That on and after Monday the 22nd February, 1943, to the end of the present session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence at every sitting over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
Civil Service

Questions will be the first item on the order of proceedings, and then that motion will be the next. On the order paper of to-day hon. members will see, under government notices of motions, reference to certain motions. One is in the name of the Prime Minister with respect to the committee on privileges and elections investigating the holding of an election for the electoral district of Stanstead. That would be the second item.
There is a notice standing in the naipe of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) for the establishment of a committee in connection with the defence of Canada regulations. That will be the third item. There is a motion standing in the name of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) for a committee on reconstruction and reestablishment. That will be the fourth item. If we conclude with these and there is time, we might take the first resolution under government orders, with respect to the $100,000 grant to the city of Ottawa. I think that will probably fill up Monday. There will be two other motions on the order paper for the appointment of committees, one on radio broadcasting and the other on railways and, shipping. If we make better progress than at the moment I anticipate, we might be prepared to take them also.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 6.05 p.m.
Monday, February 22, 1943
